title: Inquest into baby deaths hears 'birth keeper' had no medical training
text:
A coronial inquest has heard a woman who operated as a "birth keeper" for more than two decades had no medical training but instead relied on her own experience and conversations with Indigenous elders, shamans, fellow birth keepers and grandmothers.

Sita Kali, 49, was the birth keeper at two freebirths in northern NSW that are being examined at a coronial inquest into the death of four babies.

Today she was questioned about a video that was played to the court last week showing her answering questions about freebirthing and things that could go wrong during the process.

"Plenty of things can go wrong if you want to create things to go wrong," she said in the video.

Ms Kali said areas of concern she would usually cover when talking to a family included "baby being stuck, baby not breathing and haemorrhaging".

"All of those three topics I cover during pregnancy, so we don't have any of those problems," she said in the video.

"What causes baby being stuck is being stuck in the mind, not being in their physical body and doing all the preparation that I get [the mothers] to do.

"I cover how to be unstuck mainly, and that is to move."

Court hears witness 'never carried oxygen'

Ms Kali said baby not breathing was "always a big concern and why many midwives like to carry oxygen".

"I never have carried oxygen in 23 years," she said in the video.

"I guess it's more around this whole idea that it's just a physiological process.

" So I have supported parents to call the spirit of their baby into the baby's body. "

Ms Kali said there had been some babies that did not breathe "for a very long time".

"But they are always connected to the placenta, and they're always getting oxygen from that placenta," she said.

"Baby always does breathe."

Sita Kali is giving evidence at a coronial inquest. (Instagram: Mumma Sita Birthkeeper)

Ms Kali was present at the birth of Baby R, who was born at 43 weeks' gestation in 2022, and died from complications arising from "severe post-maturity".

She was also at the birth of Baby D, who died in 2024 following the stillbirth of his twin. The cause of death was believed to be twin-to-twin transfusion, a complication arising from sharing a placenta.

Counsel Assisting the Coroner, Ragni Mathur SC, today questioned the witness about the video, which was taken by Heather Bruce, a healer Ms Kali called "her mentor".

Ms Mathur said the video was published to Ms Bruce's website, and later published by the ABC in November 2024.

Ms Kali was asked whether the video represented views on birthing that she "honestly held".

She agreed, but said she thought it was a "private conversation" and did not think it would be published.

Ms Kali said it was taken out of context, and she had been "put on the spot".

She said her comments were based on her experience of working with "healthy women".

The inquest is examining the neonatal deaths of four babies between 2022 and 2024. (Image: ekseaborn0)

Ms Kali said that emotional, historical trauma could influence and impact birth, and she recommended massage, exercises and yoga to help the "physical body and mind to align".

Counsel assisting asked Ms Kali whether evidence provided to the court, which included the video and other promotional material, could lead the community to think she had clinical training and more extensive knowledge about birthing.

Ms Mathur quoted promotional material where Ms Kali called herself a "traditional midwife".

The former birth keeper told the court she had no medical qualifications and had not completed a doula's course.

"Midwifery is as old as humans. Clinical midwifery is modern medicine," she said.

The Coroner's Court inquest at Lismore is in its second week. (ABC News)

The inquest is examining the neonatal deaths of three babies born by freebirth in northern NSW, and a fourth born by homebirth in the Hunter Valley, between 2022 and 2024.

A freebirth means a baby was born without medical assistance, often supported by family, friends, a doula or "birth keeper".

Homebirths are deliveries supported by a registered midwife outside a clinical setting.

Deputy State Coroner Joan Baptie is hearing evidence about the advice and treatment given to the babies' mothers, before, during, and after the births, and how it influenced their birthing decisions.

The counsel assisting the coroner said the inquiry did not seek to place blame on the parents for their decisions but rather sought to understand the barriers preventing parents from engaging with health services.

The inquest continues.

title: NSW regional and interstate trains could be offline for a week from Friday
text:
Regional and interstate passenger train services across NSW will be suspended for a week from Friday unless a last-ditch effort to stave off proposed industrial action is successful.

Rail workers plan to walk off the job following six months of enterprise bargaining negotiations between the Australian Rail Track Corporation (ARTC) and the Rail, Tram and Bus Union (RTBU) and Australian Services Union (ASU).

Impacted train services include regional routes, interstate XPT services between Sydney, Melbourne and Brisbane, and Sydney Trains services on the Hunter Line and Southern Highlands Line.

Freight movements leading into Christmas are set to be impacted. (Supplied: Australasian Railway Association)

ARTC said the work bans would mean the safe passage of passenger trains could not be guaranteed, forcing the suspension of passenger services across its network.

"Without work-on-track authorities, ARTC cannot be assured that its people can safely access the live rail corridor to undertake essential inspections, maintenance and repairs or respond to potentially dangerous track defects," an ARTC spokesperson said in a statement.

"The restrictions arising from the notified industrial action could also compromise ARTC’s ability to respond to a safety-related incident involving a passenger service.

" This is a risk ARTC is not prepared to accept. "

As part of the industrial action, coal and freight trains would alternate days of operation over the seven-day period.

"Significant disruption to freight services is also expected, with national consequences for supply chains and the movement of essential goods at one of the busiest times of the year," the spokesperson said.

"ARTC is implementing contingency arrangements and working closely with customers to minimise disruption."

Bid to block strike

ARTC has lodged an application with the Fair Work Commission seeking a three-month suspension of protected industrial action on safety and economic grounds, with an urgent hearing requested for Thursday.

NSW TrainLink, which is not involved with the enterprise agreement dispute, said it would contact passengers with bookings with us to "secure bookings on next available services or provide refunds".

"All our regional lines, like out to Dubbo, Griffith, Moree for example, will not be able to operate and as a consequence we are now working to secure coaches for those passengers that have current bookings for that week," NSW TrainLink chief executive Roger Weeks said.

"We'll make our best effort to still get them where they need to go.

title: Construction underway on temporary transmission towers for Eyre Peninsula
text:
The southern Eyre Peninsula is expected to be reconnected to the national electricity grid by Friday morning, after storm activity last week downed two transmission towers and severely damaged a third.

More than 20,000 properties on the peninsula and West Coast lost power on Thursday during the severe weather, and while construction has begun on temporary towers, operators say it could take a year for permanent structures to be installed.

The damaged towers were located on a farm at Wharminda, which sits along a 270-kilometre transmission line between Port Lincoln and Cultana.

Construction of four temporary transmission towers has began. (ABC Eyre Peninsula: Jodie Hamilton)

Electricity transmission operator ElectraNet said local generation restored power for Port Lincoln and surrounding areas on Thursday night, and the network had to be reconfigured to allow services to return to some other parts of the Eyre Peninsula.

Following their installation, the four temporary towers would need to be tested before being re-energised, which would restore transmission services from Cultana to Port Lincoln.

ElectraNet chief executive Simon Emms said he was hoping services would be operational by early Friday.

ElectraNet's Alex Trento and Simon Emms spoke from the Eyre Peninsula on Wednesday. (ABC Eyre Peninsula: Jodie Hamilton)

"We're actually going to put up temporary towers each side of the existing line route, and then route the existing conductors around that," he said.

" The current line is down, the temporary towers are lying flat, they'll be erected today. "

SA Power Networks had advised residents in and around Port Lincoln of a planned power outage occurring on Thursday night while the region is reconnected to the transmission network.

Mr Emms said the temporary towers have been built to the same standard as the current line.

ElectraNet confident in tower design

Mr Emms said on Wednesday the three transmission towers were damaged by a "localised, very severe wind event", and he was confident they had been built to the right strength.

"We know the towers are designed to the appropriate Australian standard. That design has been checked, independently checked, and we also built a test tower and tested it to destruction," he said.

" To the best of our knowledge, it's purely that the winds were stronger than the towers were designed to withstand. "

Mr Emms said ElectraNet would undertake a "thorough and complete" investigation into the incident.

Following the storms last week, ElectraNet had suggested the towers were likely brought down by a "one-in-2,000-year weather event", something the SA government said would form part of investigations into the incident.

Damage to ElectraNet's transmission towers on the Eyre Peninsula. (ABC News: Steve Opie)

Mr Emms said new permanent transmission towers would need to be built in place of the three damaged structures, which he estimated could take up to a year.

"One of the longest lead times is actually getting all of the right steel together to build that," he said.

ElectraNet executive Alex Trento said Port Lincoln residents would need to continue to leave their rooftop solar inverters off until told otherwise, to prevent the generator coming offline before the transmission line had been restored.

title: Door not closed on capital gains carve-out for businesses as inquiry confirmed
text:
A push to exempt every active business from Labor's new capital gains tax regime is headed for a Senate inquiry, despite Treasury's strong reservations about the idea.

The proposal by independent MP Allegra Spender would apply a flat 40 per cent capital gains tax discount to all active assets, a term that captures anything used, or ready to use, to operate a business.

Mr Chalmers wrote a letter to Ms Spender last week saying her idea would not be "simpler, fairer, or enhance productivity" compared to his proposal, which applies a discount tied to inflation, with a narrower carve-out for "innovative" businesses.

But while he repeated those concerns in Question Time on Wednesday, Mr Chalmers said an inquiry was "a possible outcome".

A senior government source went further and said it was all but certain and would soon be confirmed.

The government struck a deal with the Greens on Wednesday to pass the 30 per cent minimum tax on discretionary trusts, another key budget measure. Multiple sources with knowledge of Senate negotiations said that was the government's main priority.

While Mr Chalmers has given no direct indication that he is open to amending his innovation carve-out along the lines of Ms Spender's proposal, an inquiry would push the matter into next year and make that a distinct possibility.

Where to carve the line?

The debate stems from the anger of the startup sector about the May budget decision to apply the new inflation discount to businesses and shares, not just to housing.

Startups said an inflation discount would leave them worse off than the existing 50 per cent discount, because an inflation discount is calculated based on the starting cost of an asset. Startups without physical assets often begin near zero, meaning no discount.

Chalmers sends Spender CGT letter The minor party's support will be critical to pass a minimum tax on trusts and a carve-out for start-ups in the capital gains tax regime.

The government acknowledged these concerns in budget week and promised to consult on an alternative.

The innovative business carve-out was the result, giving any eligible business younger than 15 years the choice between the new discount and the old one.

But Ms Spender and some business groups said this was too narrow and that deciding which businesses were "innovative" would be too subjective.

Ms Spender said a flat 40 per cent discount for active assets would be simpler and raise similar revenue.

In his letter, Mr Chalmers outlined three main concerns, informed by Treasury analysis. The first was that a flat 40 per cent discount would see business pay more tax in some circumstances than under an inflation discount.

The second was an integrity concern that a business would be deemed "active" as long as 80 per cent of its assets are active, creating a loophole for people to put large passive assets such as properties into otherwise-active businesses to escape the tax.

The third was a complexity concern that businesses and their shareholders would need to maintain an ongoing list of which assets were active and which were not, adding a layer of red tape to the tax system that does not currently exist.

Can the gap be bridged?

Ms Spender has discussed the idea in private with Mr Chalmers, as both have publicly indicated, and also with Prime Minister Anthony Albanese.

Ms Spender has indicated that she is receptive to modifying her proposal to address the integrity concerns.

The concern that some businesses could pay more tax could be addressed by simply allowing them to choose between the old discount and a 40 per cent discount, similar to Labor's current proposal. It's unclear how the complexity issue could be solved.

Ms Spender has emphasised the support from many business groups for her proposal, including the Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry.

She has argued that the government could repair its troubled relationship with businesses and their advocates.

The Coalition has attacked Ms Spender's idea, with Shadow Treasurer Tim Wilson going so far as to liken her to Neville Chamberlain, the British prime minister best known for appeasing Adolf Hitler, an analogy Mr Chalmers has said was not "appropriate".

Loading

The Greens have suggested they are open to considering Ms Spender's proposal, but have no major issues with the government's innovation exemption.

The minor party agreed to pass trust laws on Wednesday in exchange for extra funds for the Australian Tax Office and the Charities Commissioner to scrutinise donations made from trusts to private schools, religious organisations and others.

On the capital gains issue, Mr Chalmers told the parliament on Wednesday he would welcome a debate. "I genuinely appreciate all the engagement on this issue," he said.

"There's a range of views, including in the business community, about the government's objectives and the government's policy. In this regard, we take them seriously."

title: Khawaja says he offered Sandpapergate peace proposal
text:
Usman Khawaja has revealed he proposed a "middle ground" peace deal to Todd Greenberg that could end the Sandpapergate feud that has ripped Australian cricket apart.

Speaking on The Grade Cricketer Podcast, Khawaja read out a text message he sent to Greenberg, the CEO of Cricket Australia (CA), that he hoped the entire squad could stand behind.

"We accept and acknowledge as a team that we knew we were ball tampering by artificially altering the condition of the ball in South Africa in 2018," Khawaja's proposed statement read.

"Whether it was sandpaper, or by any other means, is irrelevant. We knew what we were doing, and we take full responsibility as a team and squad for our actions, something we should have done eight years ago.

"Furthermore, we would like to acknowledge that Steven [Smith], Cameron [Bancroft] and David [Warner] paid an enormous price for the sake of the team for which we are sorry and eternally grateful."

Khawaja said he wrote the statement after thinking about the situation last Friday.

"I was driving to the mosque on Friday … and I was reflecting and thinking about, can we not just find a middle ground?" Khawaja said.

"I don't even care any more about what they say, what we say.

"Everything is just being drip-fed right now, and it feels like there's no end to it."

He even admitted that he had a "pipe dream" that the entire squad would take accountability one day.

Khawaja said Greenberg was initially receptive to the idea, but was not convinced that the statement would solve the issue, and said he would put it to "the other parties" involved.

In a wide-ranging interview on the cult podcast, Khawaja touched on multiple topics, including the threats he has received that meant he required a security guard at a charity cricket game in Cairns on Sunday.

Usman Khawaja said he still loves Pat Cummins. (Getty Images: Quinn Rooney, file photo)

Khawaja said Pat Cummins's comments in his press conference were "really surprising" and that he had texted the Australian captain before his press conference in an attempt to try and find the middle ground.

"I was never expecting him to come out and attack me personally like that," he said.

"Attack what I said? Yeah. Personally, the way he did, for so long and he kept going and going and going I've never seen that side of Pat before.

"I didn't want to watch it, but I had to watch it. I wanted to turn it off so many times.

"I will always love Pat, and as much as he hurt me, I'm not going to judge him on a presser."

Khawaja said that he is "not convinced" that anyone else would have spoken about it when justifying the Sandpapergate chapter of his book, adding that he could understand why some people were angry that he wrote about the topic when some of his teammates were still playing.

"100 per cent, I definitely can. I'm not an idiot, I'm not devoid of empathy," he said.

"I get that side, and that's why I'm so happy now that CA has come out and said there's not going to be any sanctions, nobody's going to get in trouble, Pat Cummins remains as captain — I was actually really happy with that.

"I don't want to hurt anyone individually."

Usman Khawaja says he wants there to be a middle ground found. (Getty Images: Eurasia Sport Images/Ayush Kumar)

Khawaja said that had he come out and spoken during his career he would have never played for Australia again.

"If I'm being brutally honest, if I came out and said that while I was playing, 100 per cent my career was over," he said.

"I couldn't play for Australia anymore.

"I'm not trying to hide from that. Call me selfish, maybe it was.

"The thing I've tried to do … is talk about Cameron Bancroft. How much longer do I wait? What do I do? Do I make him suffer for another five years?"

Khawaja said that he knew sandpaper was being used on the field in Port Elizabeth, now known as Gqeberha, just by looking at the wear on the ball that was not consistent with normal wear and tear of a game.

Khawaja said he delayed coming on the podcast, he missed two previous appointments, because his appearances clashed with Pat Cummins's press conference and Cameron Bancroft's revealing West Australian article.

"I just thought that, if I came on at that time, I would inflame the situation so much more," he said.

"This was never about me versus Pat [Cummins], and I know that's what the media wanted but that was never my goal.

"As disappointed as I was about that presser, I was just, 'I'm going to stay away from this'.

"The Bancroft situation was the same … it was so deep, it was so full on."

title: Queensland and Canberra clash over environmental law review 'stunt'
text:
Federal environment minister Murray Watt says Queensland is "no longer the smart state, it's the slow state" as a stoush erupts over environmental laws.

The Commonwealth passed long-awaited overhauls to environmental approvals late last year.

The Queensland government raised concerns about the changes, and in April tasked the state's Productivity Commission to review their impact on the local infrastructure pipeline.

An interim report today revealed its final assessment would be delayed by three months, with the Commission unable to properly review the overhaul.

"Several reforms are yet to be drafted, shared for consultation or implemented," the report stated.

"As a result, there is limited observable evidence on the impacts of the reforms in their entirety."

However, Treasurer David Janetzki claimed it was clear the changes were "adding cost and delay".

In response, the federal environment minister, who is a Queensland senator, took aim at the state government, labelling the exercise a "political stunt".

"Other states are about to sign agreements with our government to reduce red tape and speed up project approvals," Senator Watt said.

"Instead, Queensland has chosen to slow down projects, waiting for a do-nothing productivity report on laws that haven't even fully begun.

" Under the Crisafulli Government, Queensland is no longer the smart state, it's the slow state. "

The interim report noted a complete assessment of the sweeping federal changes "may not be achievable for several years".

Queensland's "Smart State" slogan and trademarks were retired in 2012 under then-premier Campbell Newman's LNP government.

Extension not delay

Mr Janetzki labelled the Commission's report "startling".

He seized on findings the federal environmental laws were seeing approvals take an average of 1,150 days in the state, costing up to $7.7 billion a year.

However, the report noted this was prior to the 2025 reforms being implemented.

David Janetzki says Canberra's changes are "adding cost and delay". (ABC News: Luke Bowden)

Mr Janetzki's office said it was important to establish a baseline for comparison.

He denied the final report had been delayed, labelling it an extension, and defended its work.

"The Productivity Commission report was always about making sure Queensland was in the best position to negotiate with the federal government," he said.

"Anything that improves productivity in Queensland is an important investment, and the Productivity Commission, through all those inquiries and reporting that they are doing, is helping arm the government with productivity measures.

"Queensland's doing it. The federal government isn't."

The cost of the 15-month inquiry was not disclosed, and the treasurer said it was baked into the Commission's $6.7 million annual budget.

Deficiencies in reforms

After going largely unchanged for more than 20 years, the federal environmental laws were widely acknowledged as not fit for purpose, but a years-long stalemate in Canberra delayed their passage.

The laws aimed to cut approval times for major projects, while implementing clear environmental standards and safeguards.

New environment laws may help or hinder Ambiguous language in draft national environment laws means acting on scientific facts or not will come down to ministerial discretion.

The Productivity Commission report found while the reforms were ongoing, there were "several deficiencies".

It found some elements lacked consultation, resulting in greater costs for the agricultural sector.

"New land clearing requirements mean the scope of regulation has effectively expanded, capturing small and family farming businesses," the report stated.

"The Commission estimates the expanded requirements could cost the Queensland agriculture industry between $14 million and $41 million per year, while introducing unintended consequences for routine land management and some environmental outcomes."

Stakeholders are invited to submit their feedback on the interim report before a final report is delivered in July next year.

title: Mandatory lead testing of childcare centres in Broken Hill
text:
Early learning centres in Broken Hill will undergo mandatory testing for lead contamination following the announcement of a new multi-agency committee.

The testing will apply to all childcare services for 0-5-year-olds in the remote mining city, with remediation provided where needed.

Testing was previously an opt-in service for early learning services, which could then choose to have remediation work carried out.

Remediation is a process of making buildings and spaces lead-free through methods such as sealing windows and doors, and laying grass to trap dirt.

Testing will begin this month and continue into next year, with services to be contacted to make individual arrangements.

A new expert panel will decide when remediation is funded, based on how exposed children are to areas with elevated lead levels.

Lead contamination spreads across Broken Hill via windblown dust from the slag heap of the original mine. (ABC Broken Hill: Rhys Carman)

Broken Hill faces a historical lead pollution problem, sitting around one of the world's largest ore bodies of lead, silver and zinc.

It has been mined continuously for almost 140 years, resulting in the widespread distribution of lead in soil and dust throughout Broken Hill and surrounding areas.

Exposure to lead can cause learning disabilities, behavioural problems, slow or abnormal growth, poor coordination and hearing problems.

Children under five are particularly vulnerable because their brains are still developing.

Lead testing will now be mandatory at all early learning centres. (ABC News: Bill Ormonde)

Broken Hill mother Alisha McInerney has three-year-old twins and said the decision to conduct mandatory testing was important.

Ms McInerney said there was a lack of information after her son Hendrix had recorded above-normal blood lead levels.

"I was a little bit concerned, but we weren't really given anything, any tools to help lower them besides washing hands thoroughly."

Alisha McInerney with her twins Hendrix and Niya. (ABC Broken Hill: Em Jensen)

She said she is worried about the impact of the lead, such as developmental delays, as her children grow older.

"It is becoming such a normal thing here in Broken Hill to just accept that lead levels and regular lead testing is normal.

"I don't know any different as a parent."

Three-year-old Hendrix McInerney recorded above-average blood lead levels. (ABC Broken Hill: Em Jensen)

Interim chief executive of the NSW Environment Protection Authority (EPA) Nancy Chang said in a statement that despite a drop in Broken Hill blood lead levels by more than 75 per cent in children under 5, they are still too high.

"We know that children under 5 years of age are more likely to be at risk of harm from lead because of their hand-to-mouth behaviour, touching and crawling on dusty surfaces and their young bodies absorbing a higher proportion of lead than adults as they grow," Ms Chang said.

According to the latest Annual Lead Program Report from NSW Ministry of Health, 35 per cent of children aged one to five, and 56 per cent of Aboriginal children, have blood lead levels above the national health investigative guideline of 5 micrograms per decilitre (5 µg/dL).

Testing of childcare centres conducted by the NSW EPA between 2015 and 2025 found high lead contamination levels at 10 facilities, but parents were not informed.

The new mandatory testing and clean-up will be conducted under a new Broken Hill Lead Coordination Committee, coordinated by the NSW EPA and including NSW Health and the Department of Education, expected to be running by early 2027.

Cartoon character Lead Ted advises children to wash their hands after playing on equipment at a public park in Broken Hill. (ABC Broken Hill: Em Jensen)

In January, a report from the Office of the Chief Scientist and Engineer (OCSE) made four main recommendations around coordination, data and program evaluation, public health initiatives, remediation, and emissions control to address lead contamination in the city.

The NSW government has now accepted all recommendations.

NSW Health Minister Ryan Park said today that more could and should still be done to tackle the issue.

"It's not an area that we should set and forget, though, to be honest. It's an area we should continue to look at and examine," Mr Park said.

"We've got to make sure our communities are as safe as possible not matter where they are."

A caution sign for hazardous lead in Broken Hill. (ABC Broken Hill: Em Jensen)

NSW Greens MP and mining spokesperson Cate Faehrmann welcomed the announcement, though she said it was "long-overdue but also too little, too late".

"It's outrageous that government agencies knew young children were being exposed to dangerous levels of lead and failed to act immediately.

"The fact that generations of Broken Hill children have been exposed to lead contamination on this scale is a national disgrace."

The NSW government put aside $37 million in funding earlier this year to double the number of homes remediated in the city each year and support ongoing testing for children, particularly Aboriginal children.

title: Matildas keeper reveals career-threatening health scare
text:
A neurological disorder threatened to cut Teagan Micah's career short, but the Australian goalkeeper has overcome it with a little help from her Matildas friends.

The 29-year-old was diagnosed with autonomic dysfunction after suffering a concussion in March while training with her current French club, Lyon.

She previously sustained a serious head injury in 2022 with Swedish side FC Rosengård and the latest concussion forced the shot stopper to miss March's Asian Cup.

It also led to her developing the debilitating condition, which stops the nervous system properly regulating automatic body functions.

Micah has recovered and returns to Joe Montemurro's Matildas squad for their two-game series against Colombia, beginning in Canberra on Saturday night.

Speaking to reporters on Wednesday, the Queensland product revealed the "big health scare" threatened to force her into early retirement.

"I had a lot of chats with my family, with doctors, my best friends … every day about retirement, and it was looking like that for a while," Micah said.

Teagan Micah plays for OL Lyonnes in the French top flight. (Getty Images: Eurasia Sport Images/Lilou Cassin)

She experienced problems regulating her heart rate, which would rise to 190 beats per minute after walking for 2 minutes.

Micah consulted with specialists in Sydney, Geneva and France in a bid to get healthy and back on the field.

"It was probably about June, July time when I came home to [Australia] for about two weeks and I also saw my doctors here … it was kind of the turning point for me," she said.

"I sat down with my family and spoke a lot with them [about retiring] and it was just a matter of … get back healthy first and then making the decision.

"I didn't want to make a decision before that because I knew it wasn't going to be something I'd be comfortable with … I just knew I wanted to keep going."

Micah, who says she feels "alive again", credited ex-Lyon star Ellie Carpenter and other Australian teammates for getting her back on her feet.

"She got me through so many days," Micah said of close friend Carpenter.

"She sent me food to my apartment when I couldn't get out of bed for days.

"Steph [Catley], Ellie, Ras [Hayley Raso] were the main ones checking in all the time.

Hayley Raso (left) was one of Teagan Micah's key supporters during her lay-off. (Getty Images: Paul Kane)

"Also the coaching staff here, the Matildas, were incredible as well … and at Lyon, those girls made me smile on days where I didn't think I had it in me anymore."

Competing with Mackenzie Arnold for the number 1 shirt, Micah said she would do everything possible to nab a spot in Australia's squad for the 2027 World Cup in Brazil.

"I need to probably go back to the drawing board and write down what I want to achieve now with the rest of my career," Micah said.

"Now that I feel good and I'm ready to go it's like where do I want my career to take me … [I want] to use this second chance I have."

The friendlies in Canberra and Geelong are world number 15 Australia's last before the World Cup draw on December 11.

World number 19 Colombia have established themselves as the second-best South American team behind hosts Brazil.

Along with Micah, Australia have regained Mary Fowler, Kyra Cooney-Cross, Alanna Kennedy, Tameka Yallop and Kahli Johnson.

Everton attacker Holly McNamara [hamstring] is out until late December, while Clare Hunt and Charlie Rule remain sidelined.

After her son was born, Lynn Baker couldn’t get the thought of his pram rolling under a train out of her head. Baker, 46, is a single mother by choice and her anxiety was already high by the time she became pregnant, due to a difficult IVF process. Intrusive thoughts about harming her son Micah, who is now two years old, only worsened during her first year of motherhood. Another thought that plagued her was accidentally banging Micah’s head on the kitchen counter. Lynn Baker and son Micah. Sam Mooy Looking back on this time, she remembers asking herself: “It’s not my intent, but am I going to do that?”

“I didn’t, at one point, know if I could trust myself to be alone with my son, and that was so devastating, right, because my son was also my dream come true,” she says. Editor's pick Fertility Sam wanted a baby. This diagnosis cost him $90,000 and his relationship And Baker is far from alone. UNSW recently conducted a research survey of 439 people who had given birth one to six months ago. Participants reported that 95 per cent had thoughts about accidentally harming their baby. Researchers Jodie Pestana and Susanne Schweizer say this survey is part of a larger body of work yet to come on perinatal mental health. Schweizer says intrusive thoughts are common and while more evidence is needed about why they occur, the leading theory is that they are evolutionary.

“Imagine you’re out on a high-rise balcony with a newborn thrust into your arms, and you have an intrusive thought of the baby accidentally falling over the railing. You’re probably taking a step back,” says Schweizer. Fifty-four per cent of survey respondents reported intrusive thoughts about intentionally harming their baby, and one in five reported severe or extreme distress about having these thoughts. Schweizer says thoughts of intentional harm are still normal and are not associated with an increased risk to the baby, unless they occur with postpartum psychosis, a condition which affects less than one per cent of people. Once new mum Lynn Baker started talking about her intrusive thoughts, they became less powerful. Sam Mooy Schweizer emphasises the normalcy of the thoughts but also how confronting the experience can be for new parents, particularly if they are unaware of them.

Advertisement

As a psychologist and mother herself, Schweizer wasn’t prepared. “You think, ‘Why is my brain producing this thought?’ Speaking from experience as a mum of three, this is so in contrast with every single thing you’re feeling about this infant and about being their mother, it’s the furthest thing from what you actually would want to do. “I hope that no mum has to have these thoughts in the future and not know what they are,” says Schweizer. Narelle Dickinson, a perinatal psychologist and director of Lotus Health and Psychology in Brisbane, agrees that intrusive thoughts are harmless until they cause consistent distress. While there are no rules about when to seek help, diagnostically, Dickinson says the general timeframe is distress lasting about two or more weeks.

Advertisement

Editor's pick Sex & relationships ‘I still haven’t heard I love you’: Why many young people have never been in a relationship “What I normally say is everyone has bad days or maybe you’re having a tough afternoon because baby won’t settle, unfortunately that’s the life of a new parent. But when you are having more of those tough days than good days then it’s time to check in with someone on your healthcare team or even a loved one,” says Dickinson. When Baker was struggling, she was reluctant to ask for help, fearing being judged or having her worst fears come true and being deemed an unsafe mother. “I asked my GP, ‘Are they going to take my son away from me?’” When asking for help, it’s OK if the healthcare professional doesn’t understand perinatal intrusive thoughts, says Dickinson.

Advertisement

“If you seek help, and they react as if what you’ve said is terrible, or they want to take the baby because they don’t think you’re safe, they might not understand intrusive thoughts. If they react like this, talk to someone else,” says Dickinson. Researchers Pestana and Schweizer say this is one of the key reason for research like theirs, as a foundation to train clinicians, particularly as mental health disorders climb in pregnancy. According to a recently published national report from the Gidget Foundation and Women’s Mental Health Australia, perinatal anxiety and depression is increasing, with one in four mothers experiencing anxiety or depression. Baker says if a doctor had told her about the possibility of intrusive thoughts, she might not have been as stressed. Eventually, she found herself Googling and found an explanation that confirmed she “wasn’t crazy”. The thoughts also generally get worse when they are bottled up. And Baker agrees she started to feel relief when she spoke about the things running through her mind.

Advertisement

“The minute you start talking about the thoughts, they diminish, right, they become less powerful.” Make the most of your health, relationships, fitness and nutrition with our Live Well newsletter. Get it in your inbox every Monday.

The Cook government has banned Deloitte from winning government contracts for three months as the fallout continues over the company’s error-riddled partly AI-generated report into the controversial university merger proposal. The government was left embarrassed last month after Redditors found serious errors and AI hallucinations in Deloitte’s report, which the government held up as proof of the need to pursue a three-way merger between UWA, Curtin and Murdoch. Deloitte has been banned from WA government work for three months. Eamon Gallagher The AFR reported on Wednesday the government told Deloitte it would not be able to secure work for a quarter at a meeting on Wednesday. Finance Minister David Michael and Deloitte were approached for comment.

Advertisement

The ban will be a financial hit to Deloitte, which wins millions in contracts from the WA government every year. In the past few months alone it won a $2.5 million contract to provide tax services to the Government Employees Superannuation Board, a $2.1 million contract for auditing services for Gold Corporation and $1.7 million for “change management office services for the Westport program”. Tertiary and International Education Minister Tony Buti slammed the report after the errors emerged and called on Deloitte to partially refund the $166,000 it cost to produce, as well as reissue the report with the errors fixed. To date, Deloitte has not publicly confirmed it was going to pay back any money or whether it would reissue the report. On Monday, Buti hinted discussions with Deloitte were not going well.

Advertisement

“We are demanding that a refund be looked at, but if that doesn’t take place, there are other measures that we can put in place,” he said. “I’m incredibly disappointed at Deloitte. I’ve said it. Very embarrassed by what happened, but incredibly disappointed in their performance. “I can assure you, yes, we have [requested a refund] and discussions have taken place, but there hasn’t been a satisfactory outcome at this stage.” Deloitte was force to repay nearly $100,000 for a $440,000 report prepared for the Department of Employment and Workplace Relations because it was found to have used AI. The first errors identified by Reddit users were three citations that referenced wrong authors and one link that sent users to the ChatGPT website.

Advertisement

On closer inspection, users also found errors in the figures cited in the merger report. Throughout the document it identifies the three-way Curtin, Murdoch and UWA merger as delivering the largest cost benefit. However, its own summary table of the cost benefits show a two-way Murdoch and UWA merger by far offered the highest cost benefit. Another glaring error was contained in a table calculating the total cost of a Curtin and UWA merger under a high-cost scenario. The report suggests the high costs of the merger to day one was $514 million and $145 million in the five years after and suggests this was a total cost of $399 million – $260 million less than the actual total of the two figures.

Advertisement

Deloitte acknowledged AI was used in the report for “collation of research, synthesis of information and editorial proofing” but said it was all reviewed. Deloitte initially categorised the mistakes as “minor referencing errors”. Fortescue deputy chair Mark Barnaba is leading the steering committee that will probe the university merger proposals. At a breakfast on Tuesday, Barnaba said there was a compelling case for mergers. “We want our universities to be globally competitive, relevant and financially viable so that Western Australia remains the best place in the world to live, do business and get a quality job,” he said.

title: A mixed grade for deciding on the future of homework
text:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Megan Herbert Homework. We all have it, we all do it. As far as school work to be done at home, it’s absolutely a good idea, but it must be relevant and meaningful (“Skirmish shows it’s not all quiet on homework front”, November 25). What is it? Revision mostly and additional learning on your own. It’s not the amount given or time spent on it. What does it provide the teacher? Does the teacher look at it, use it, mark it? What does it do for the student? Let them know if they understood or learned anything from the class lesson? It was all these things when parents weren’t so involved and teachers actually taught.

Jenny Greenwood, Bowral Any intuitive parent and teacher knows that the benefits of homework outlined by Christopher Harris are self-evident. Education is like the economy that swung from over-regulated tariffs to the wide open spaces of free trade, resulting in pockets of privilege and pervading inequality. A balanced approach isn’t rocket science. What student hasn’t empathised with Romeo and Juliet after wading through 100 comprehension questions, but expecting a large class to “get” Shakespeare and write a polished essay in blocks of 50 minutes is equally unrealistic.

Peter Farmer, Northbridge How good is homework? Getty Images As a high school student in the 1970s I was given homework in various subjects, but I would only ever complete it for the subjects I enjoyed. As a teacher, I would set a small amount of homework maybe once a week and only in some of the subjects I taught, while some faculties would set it after nearly every lesson. I came to the conclusion that homework is beneficial, but it must be relative to what the students are studying, not take hours to do and, most importantly, be marked by the teacher and meaningful feedback given.

Peter Miniutti, Ashbury It seems this research was based on interviews with kids, parents and teachers. Hardly a basis for such a conclusion based on qualitative data with no quantitative data. Parents seeking homework which includes spelling words and maths sheets plus pursuing academic tutoring is just an extension of the school day. Kids in Early Stage 1 through to Stage 2 (K – 4) hardly need this. Parents should be focusing on instructive play, sport, talking and listening and reading. Reading to your child is perhaps the most important ″⁣homework″⁣. In later stages of schooling, homework may have its place, but allowing young children the space to relax and enjoy their parents’ company and modelling, is the best option for after school activity.

Scott Warnes, Suffolk Park Homework beats tutoring every school day of the week. Sure no student likes it, but boy does it help with reinforcing knowledge, applying key concepts, time management and self-confidence. But how did I ever get it done after playing sport all weekend, then rushing home on a Sunday night to watch Molly on Countdown? Ah, just another brick in the wall.

Michael Blissenden, Castle Hill

Advertisement

Homework sometimes becomes an ego trip for a parent. At a P&C meeting I once heard a competitive mother ask, ″⁣Well, what is our homework project for this week?″⁣ The reply was, ″⁣Read to your children and have them read to you.″⁣ A happier, uncheatable parent and student outcome, except for the one deflated ego.

Joy Cooksey, Harrington CO2 argument hot air One of your correspondents (Letters, November 25) states that “in reality land we all continue to use fossil fuels” and claims that CO2 is an elixir of life. Certainly CO2 is necessary for human life and agriculture. However, we are producing too much of it, which is having a detrimental effect on planetary systems. Anthropogenic climate change is a scientific fact, and not a political ploy by the left in politics as your correspondent suggests. A sufficient amount of CO2 is beneficial, an overabundance is not and is an existential threat to life on the planet. No scientist has claimed that CO2 is evil, but the science of global climate change was settled decades ago, we are increasingly seeing the results, it is disappointing that your correspondent misrepresents the science, and claims that emissions reductions are misguided. The $150 million spent on COP31, is a drop in the ocean compared with the cost of increasing massive storm events, floods, droughts, bushfires, and people displaced through famine. I’m afraid that the straw man argument used in the letter has no credibility.

Barrington Salter, Elanora (Qld) It seems likely that Chris Bowen will get skewered for his perceived failure to get an agreement at COP31. If so, it will be disappointing because that failure was caused by government decisions made over several decades. Australia is locked into not only fossil use but also its export to pay for the import of goods we use to manufacture, an industry killed by both sides of politics who succumbed to the entreaties of lobby groups that argued for a resource-based economy. Our imports have ballooned because of population growth and the demand created for housing and appliances like cars. Yet back in the 1970s we were exporting cars.

Don Owers, Whitebridge Taylor needs some reverse swing Angus Taylor has made it clear by his comments on the economy that we need to be rid of this rotten government(“Economic woe ’may force rate cuts by June‴⁣⁣ , November 25). Could he try some sandpaper, to assist reversing his party’s woeful performance in opposition?

Peter Willis, Orange Trump whisperer

Advertisement

We now know what Xi Jinping was whispering into Trump’s ear (″⁣Huang back at helm of Nvidia as Trump steps in″⁣, November 25).

Graham Fazio, Cootamundra Matt Golding When I saw the Trump-supplied AI image of a triumphant and bloodied Jensen Huang holding aloft a red bra (smh.com.au) I felt despair. Not only because a man who is being examined by the FBI and US intelligence agencies is depicted as a wronged, surviving hero, but that a convenient symbol of womanhood is used as a sexist prop to denote victory. I feel positive that no female CEO would ever be reinstated after having had several extramarital affairs while leader. She would be shamed as not only being promiscuous, something apparently acceptable in men but not in women, but also making a cuckold of her husband. Vale feminism. It was a valiant effort. Judy Hungerford, Narraweena Now that it’s deemed acceptable, I’m waiting for a honeypot to contact me. Tim Schroder, Gordon Inscrutable, dissolute, dodgy mates, but great hair. No, not the orange one. Kath Maher, Lidcombe Always on the alert for trouble As a former drover in the Central West during years of drought, I take exception to the slur on drovers’ dogs regarding Jensen Huang (Letters, November 25). My six smart droving dogs saved the day, every day. They were also excellent judges of character and knew a hardened rogue when they saw one. I can assure your correspondent they would never have let Jensen Huang back. They’d have given him the eye, circled him and then bailed him up for good measure. They were, after all, discerning dogs. Vivien Clark-Ferraino, Duckmaloi

Advertisement

Blame pollies for housing crisis At last, here’s someone prepared to identify the true culprits for the housing crisis (‴⁣⁣Blame all politicians, not migrants, over housing‴⁣⁣, November 25). While too many politicians spend far too much time blaming migrants for causing the crisis, Martin Parkinson, who formerly ran Treasury and the prime minister’s department, is spot on in identifying the real people responsible for the mess we’re in. Parkinson is right in saying that politicians have not been honest about their own planning failures. However, I’m unsure if they’d see the housing boom as a failure. Long gone are the days when leaders such as Chifley and Menzies believed governments had a duty to build public housing on a massive scale. Instead, subsequent leaders, John Howard in particular, introduced policies biased towards investors. It changed the way many Australians thought about housing. As former Senator Doug Cameron said many years ago, a house changed from being a home to being an investment. Many politicians themselves have benefited and own second “homes”. Long story short: today many people under the age of 40 have no chance of ever buying a house, and struggle with rising rents at a time of falling wages. It’s worse here in the Blue Mountains where hundreds of houses that were once homes to local workers are being turned over to Airbnb and other forms of short-term accommodation. It’ll take a lot of fixing. Meanwhile, the Minns government continues to sit on its review of short-term accommodation. Nick Franklin, Katoomba Martin Parkinson nails it. The politicians’ “Look over there!” xenophobic blame game only exacerbates the problems poor planning creates. When a doctor or an abattoir worker or a seasonal fruit picker is told their contribution is worthless, or they are taking up space despite having gone through a rigorous application process and been accepted for their skills – it’s time to look at the policymakers and political through-lines that devalue them and us as human beings. Beverley Fine, Pagewood Easy. Migration was so high in 2023 should always be qualified with “because there was no migration for two years during COVID”. You were all visa-ed up, but couldn’t come. And why did it “coincide with the largest jump in property prices and surge in rents”? That’s easy too – greed. And yes, no one to control that greed. Claudia Drevikovsky, Croydon It is long overdue for politicians to legislate a rent review board with powers to lower excessive rents. It is a simple fact that rents are too high. Many years ago, a young landlord on TV disclosed he had many rental properties and he simply increased rents each year. It is obvious that this mentality is now everywhere. As an initial step, all rents must be frozen. Those charging the highest rents must then be requested to justify them and reduce them if applicable. Just because the landlord is highly geared does not justify high rental. John O’Connell, Old Toongabbie Molly made us better Molly Meldrum made a positive contribution to society, encouraged young people to artistry, showed us that gay people were not hurtful and harmful, and had 20 per cent of the population watching a fun and positive show that we all talked about (Letters, November 25). Molly changed Australia for the better and deserves a state funeral. Fred Nile demonised gays and, despite his many years in parliament, it’s hard to see a positive, bright thing he stood for or did. He may have had long “public service”, most of it pushing views that the majority rejected. Reserve state funerals for those who, like Molly, represent something positive. Steven Lee, Faulconbridge

He also expressed shock at his former teammate’s writing that he was passed over to stand in for the banned Steve Smith after the Cape Town Test because “they weren’t ready for a brown Australian cricket captain, even as an interim”. Khawaja has been withdrawn from Fox Sports commentary given the tension around the sandpaper scandal and pulled out of several media commitments, and said he had done so to avoid inflaming and feeding the media cycle. Pat Cummins and Usman Khawaja together on national duty. title: Stagflation fears grip Canberra as inflation, unemployment surge
text:
Advertisement

PoliticsFederalInflation Stagflation fears grip Canberra as inflation, unemployment surge Shane Wright Updated November 25, 2026 — 6:17pm ,first published 11:57am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

There are fears Australia could be dragged into stagflation as inflation surges to its highest level since the war against Iran began, the economy slows under the weight of high interest rates and unemployment pushes beyond 5 per cent. As one of the nation’s biggest retailers, Harvey Norman, reported a sharp fall in profit and Reserve Bank research revealed even people unaffected by rate rises are cutting back on essentials, data from the bureau of statistics showed annual inflation hit 4.9 per cent in October. Petrol prices grew by 6.3 per cent in the month of October. Louie Douvis In seasonally adjusted terms, prices across the country lifted by 0.7 per cent last month with half of the jump due to the surge in oil prices. Of concern to the Reserve Bank, underlying inflation lifted by a more-than-expected 3.5 per cent to take the annual rate to 3.8 per cent. The numbers were a further blow to the government, which continues to struggle in opinion polls, and to Treasurer Jim Chalmers, who earlier this week warned the economy would slow and the jobless rate would push above 5 per cent.

Advertisement

Chalmers described the result as “another unwelcome but unsurprising reminder” of the financial pressures facing all Australians. He said next month’s mid-year budget update would contain spending cuts aimed at helping put downward pressure on inflation, signalling infrastructure projects may be delayed or axed completely. “From budget update to budget update, it’s not unusual for projects to be re-profiled sometimes for a whole range of reasons, including pressures on the workforce and pressures on the economy. And so, those sorts of discussions are part of the work that will happen between now and the release of the mid-year update,” he said. HSBC Australia chief economist Paul Bloxham said the economy was showing clear signs of stagflation, which is when economic growth slows and inflation is high.

Advertisement

“As each data release has arrived over recent weeks, Australia’s economy is looking more and more like it is moving into stagflation,” he said. He was backed by BDO chief economist Anders Magnusson who noted unemployment had reached 4.9 per cent in October with fewer people in work and those holding down a job employed for fewer hours. “The economy is showing signs of stagflation,” he said. The bureau reports that the cost of building new homes lifted 0.8 per cent through the month to be 5.1 per cent higher over the year. Rent inflation actually slowed to 3.5 per cent, its lowest annual rate since the pandemic. Petrol prices grew by 6.3 per cent in October after a 9.4 per cent jump in September. Over the past 12 months, prices for petrol and diesel have soared by 32.5 per cent.

Advertisement

The cost of eating out has climbed by 4.1 per cent, while fruit and vegetable prices lifted by 7.5 per cent. That is being pushed by a surge in fruit prices which have risen by 10.9 per cent over the year. There were large increases in the prices for clothing and footwear, plus household goods, which both increased by 1.2 per cent. Both are heavily influenced by changes in the Australian dollar. Electricity prices have fallen since January but are up by 25 per cent over the past 12 months because of federal government power subsidies, which ended last October. Shadow treasurer Tim Wilson said government spending was driving inflation, accusing Chalmers of losing control of the economy.

Advertisement

“We have persistent government-driven inflation by spending, and the treasurer keeps putting his foot down on the accelerator by continuing to stoke spending as part of his active inflation agenda,” he said. Related Article Australian economy What is a recession and are we in one? A bluffer’s guide Despite the figures, most economists believe this will be the high point for inflation as lower oil prices start feeding through the economy. Financial markets still expect the RBA to hold rates through to the middle of 2027 and begin to cut in August. AMP deputy chief economist Diana Mousina said inflation had probably peaked, with petrol prices down 20 per cent in the past four weeks, rents were slowing while wage pressures would ease because of higher unemployment. The slowdown in household spending is evident in the retail sector. Harvey Norman on Wednesday reported a 47 per cent fall in profits before tax for the period between July and October compared with the same period last year.

Advertisement

“There’s no one in the shop,” the chain’s executive chairman Gerry Harvey told this masthead. “Every retailer I talk to is in a similar situation … And if they’re under pressure now, it’s only going to get worse next year.” It joins other retailers such as Nick Scali, Bunnings and David Jones to have reported a drop in sales since the Reserve started tightening monetary policy. RBA research, released on Wednesday, revealed higher interest rates are forcing people even without a mortgage to curb their spending. It found 72 per cent of people with a mortgage had cut spending, with 41 per cent cutting expenditure on essentials while 54 per cent had reduced outlays on non-essentials. Renters were also keeping their wallets shut, with 62 per cent cutting their expenditure overall, 35 per cent slicing spending on essentials and 39 per cent shifting to lower-priced goods.

Advertisement

Even those who own their home outright report belt-tightening since the RBA started lifting rates. A fifth of this group said they had cut spending on essentials while 29 per cent said they had delayed expenditure on non-essentials. The survey was taken during September, ahead of the RBA’s decision at the end of that month and then in November to deliver back-to-back interest rate rises. Related Article Analysis

Australian economy Chalmers cannot spin a silver lining out of this grim story Some economists have put the chance of the country falling into a recession at 50-50, little better than a coin toss. But a recession may be avoided because of pent-up demand in the construction sector. Figures released on Wednesday showed the inflation-adjusted value of residential building reached an all-time high of $30.4 billion in the September quarter, a 9 per cent increase over the past year.

Advertisement

Non-residential construction, much of it building for data centres and renewable energy projects, lifted in the quarter to be 10.2 per cent stronger over the past 12 months. The residential numbers will feed into the September quarter national accounts, to be released next week, which are expected to show the economy expanded by about 0.4 per cent. Promises of local jobs at a Queensland government project in Mackay did not eventuate, with CFMEU-backed contractors from Brisbane brought in instead to upgrade the city’s hospital. Vassallo Constructions director Brendan Vassallo told the Commission of Inquiry into the CFMEU and Misconduct in the Construction Industry on Wednesday the company had sought work at the $250 million Mackay Base Hospital upgrade, which has still not been completed. BESIX Watpac had been awarded the contract to deliver the project, and Vassallo met with project director Michael Brady to discuss opportunities. title: Higher taxes on trusts set to become law after Labor secures Greens support
text:
In brief New laws will impose a minimum 30 per cent tax on some discretionary trusts.

Private jet owners will have to pay the same fuel excise rate as motorists under the new laws.

Individuals and small businesses will have to pay higher taxes on trusts after the Greens gave the proposal the support it needs to pass the Senate.

The law, announced in the government's May budget, will impose a minimum 30 per cent tax on some discretionary trusts, but will now also hit private jet owners with a higher fuel levy, as the minor party demanded.

Discretionary trusts can be used to split income, including among relatives and families running businesses — something critics argue is a way for the wealthy to dodge higher income taxes.

"Discretionary trusts are basically a legalised defrauding of the Commonwealth that is overwhelmingly exploited by super wealthy people to avoid paying their fair share," Greens treasury spokesperson Nick McKim told reporters on Wednesday.

"At the end of the day, today Australia's tax system will just be a little bit fairer, and it will be fairer because we are cracking down on the 1 per cent."

Private jet owners will now pay the same fuel excise rate as motorists: 53.7 cents a litre, up from 3.56 cents per litre of aviation fuel.

The Greens had hoped Labor would agree to close a loophole for non-taxpaying entities like private schools, religious institutions and sporting clubs, but the parties instead struck a deal.

The tax office would now be able to better target trust distributions to "cults" and charities without a deductible recipient endorsement, according to McKim.

"There will be extra resources for the ATO ... there will also be stronger probity frameworks that will be able to be enforced," he said.

Small businesses and industry groups had forecast a $1 billion hit if the changes took effect, pleading with the government to abandon the proposal amid a cost of living crisis.

The Business Council of Australia had said employers would be hit twice — once to comply with the new rules and a second time when they paid the higher tax.

The Coalition opposed the measures over businesses' concerns, leaving the Greens as Labor's sole negotiating partner in the upper house.

The trust tax concessions are the latest in a volley of recent wins for the minor party, who snagged changes to the government's digital duty of care laws on Tuesday and landed a deal to carve out pensioners from cuts to private health insurance rebates.

title: Australia's inflation problem is growing again. When can we expect relief?
text:
In brief The consumer price index has risen to its highest level in three years.

It comes after grim unemployment figures were released last week.

Australia's inflation numbers are heading in the wrong direction, with a shocking rise in the price of goods and services leaving the prospect of a rate cut further away.

The headline consumer price index (CPI) rose 4.9 per cent in the 12 months to October 2026, up from 4.3 per cent in the 12 months to September. It's now at its highest in three years.

It wasn't the news many Australians seeking relief after a wave of painful rate hikes this year were expecting.

The figures — including the underlying rate — even floored markets and economists who, while bracing for inflation to rise this month, did not expect it to be this high.

"This is a very serious moment for our economy, and we will respond in substantial ways," Treasurer Jim Chalmers said, reacting to the data.

Why did inflation increase in October?

Transport costs, electricity fees, and construction of new builds were the main factors behind the surge. The rise in electricity prices was due to government rebates ending, increasing the hit to consumers' pockets.

Fuel prices rose 6.3 per cent in October — averaging 246.7 cents per litre for petrol nationally — and were a major contributor to the inflation spike.

Headline inflation has hit a three-year high. Source: SBS News

It was above expectations.

Bendigo Bank chief economist David Robertson said while the headline 4.9 per cent was close to forecasts, the core rate of inflation at 3.8 per cent was above consensus.

"It is also above the [Reserve Bank's] latest forecasts, which expected core inflation to remain steady at 3.6 per cent," he said in a statement.

How is the economy faring?

There were already concerns that Australia could be heading for a recession, if not technically in one already, after grim unemployment figures were released last week.

The jobless rate is now at its highest level in five years, and is predicted to increase.

Macquarie Bank has now joined HSBC in forecasting a 50-50 chance of a recession.

Cherelle Murphy, EY's chief economist for Oceania, says it's not often that both unemployment and inflation rise.

"It's often that we get one or not the other. What we're sort of seeing at the moment is an economy which is definitely slowing down," she told ABC News.

The figures will leave the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) pondering whether the steep rise in the unemployment rate is enough — or whether the shock inflation figures will push it towards another rate hike.

"It's going to continue to grow up faster than expected, and so then the RBA is going to increasingly have to make a decision between whether they're going to set interest rates to light inflation or whether they're going to take jobs," University of Sydney economist Gareth Bryant told SBS News.

Could 2027 bring some relief??

Chalmers said despite the inflation surprise, CPI is still expected to come down to the target band in mid next year, and the economy will continue to grow.

But there will still be some painful months ahead.

"When it comes to the way that we see the year ahead, 2026 has been an especially difficult year for people. We expect this inflation for a range of reasons to hang around for a bit longer than anyone would like," he said.

The RBA's rate hikes are still filtering through the economy — so the inflation figures paint the current picture, not the future.

"This is kind of looking at the 2026 economy — it doesn't necessarily tell us what's going to go on in 2027," Murphy said.

"So yes, we will see the economy slow. Yes, we'll probably see unemployment hover around these levels and maybe even move a little higher.

"But it's what happens to inflation throughout the course of next year that matters. And as long as the Reserve Bank sees it start to come down, it's probably going to be fairly satisfied that it's done enough. If it continues to surprise on the upside because something else changed or that inflationary pressure simply isn't going away, then that's when they'll be thinking about further rate hikes."

READ MORE The money changes you can make, as Australians told to expect financial pain

Robertson anticipates the cash rate will remain unchanged when the RBA meets next month.

"I expect the official cash rate will remain steady at 4.85 per cent for most of 2027, and still expect there will likely be a longer, more drawn-out cash rate cycle than consensus," he said in a statement.

"Labour markets continue to suggest there's no need for further rate hikes. Volatile global markets are complicating the outlook again, suggesting that current rates are sufficiently restrictive."

But a rate cut by mid-2027 is now more unlikely.

"With employment softening, housing under pressure and financial conditions restrictive, we believe the bar for another hike remains high, even after this upside surprise," said Joseph Marassa, strategist at exchange-traded fund provider Global X ETFs in a statement.

"However, until price pressures are convincingly contained, rate relief may remain a distant prospect."

title: Jensen Huang’s mega-status as the world’s ‘AI bank’ raises Trump concerns
text:
In brief Jensen Huang apologised to staff as he returned to Nvidia following a scandal involving multiple affairs.

An initial market rally faded as scrutiny of the AI giant's relationship to US President Donald Trump persisted.

Jensen Huang apologised to Nvidia staff and said he was in therapy on Tuesday, as a stock rally triggered by his shock return as CEO faltered amid persistent doubts over the probes he faces and the fate of the AI investment boom.

Huang resigned on 12 November over extramarital affairs, including one with a woman some US intelligence officials suspected of being a Chinese spy. His departure sent shares in Nvidia and companies closely linked to AI tumbling.

However, after initially saying it did not intend to reinstate Huang, Nvidia's board announced the company's founder was "the right person to lead Nvidia" and his reinstatement served stockholders, employees, partners and customers.

"I made some terrible mistakes," Huang told an hour-long all-hands meeting at the company's headquarters in Santa Clara, California, the New York Times reported after reviewing a livestream of the event.

He told staff it was "not acceptable" that he had broken a code of conduct he had helped write, and dismissed suggestions that he was back because United States President Donald Trump had pressured the board.

But Trump told CNBC on Tuesday that he had been in contact with directors about Huang's return.

"I spoke to them, let me put it that way," Trump said. "And I convinced them."

After vaulting more than 30 per cent on Tuesday, Nvidia shares were down about 6 per cent at close.

"The optimism faded quickly" for Nvidia, wrote analyst Fawad Razaqzada of Forex.com, with "questions over corporate governance and board oversight still lingering".

So far, Tuesday's surge had been a "one-day wonder", according to Ken Mahoney, president and CEO of investment firm Mahoney Asset Management.

"We are not seeing an upside follow-through today at all."

Trump pressure

Trump's push for Huang's reinstatement was an intervention in the business world like no US president has done before.

"There's no precedent for any of this," Ann Lipton, a law professor at the University of Colorado Boulder, told the Agence France-Presse news agency.

According to media reports, the 80-year-old billionaire invited himself onto a conference call of Nvidia's board to plead the case of the chip giant's founder.

READ MORE Donald Trump hails Nvidia's reinstatement of CEO Jensen Huang after affair scandal

Trump assured board members that Huang would face no action from the US justice department — a promise he could make, as the department is headed by his former personal lawyer.

Trump also intervened in the Nvidia affair to halt a plunge in artificial intelligence stocks triggered by Huang's resignation, which had raised fears of a broader stock market correction.

Trump was reportedly talked into backing the return of the Taiwan-born CEO after top tech investors told him the US economy and Wall Street depended on it.

The unprecedented move breaks with the long-held US tradition of free enterprise, which rejects government intervention outright — or at least overly explicit state direction of the economy.

At the height of the financial crisis in 2009, the White House secured the departure of the head of General Motors, a carmaker then being kept afloat by government aid, but then-president Barack Obama did not boast about it.

The Nvidia case is very different.

For one thing, the US government has no financial ties to the thriving company.

Trump, however, is an investor in Nvidia, owning as many as 370,000 shares as of 30 September, according to filings.

Shares linked to the AI boom have fallen steeply in recent weeks amid fears that the AI bubble, inflated since the launch of OpenAI's ChatGPT in 2022, was finally bursting.

In downward-trending markets, quick rebounds are common but "tend to get negated and that has been the sequence since early October", Mahoney said, adding that "sellers have absolute control of the market here".

Nvidia is central to the AI investment story — its powerful processors are the key tool for training and running the AI models believed to be at the heart of a technological revolution.

The massive spending on its AI chips and software, housed in sprawling data centres, catapulted the company into the ranks of the world's most valuable firms.

Huang used that success to turn Nvidia into a kind of central bank for other AI companies and startups, doling out loans and financial guarantees to firms that would otherwise struggle to borrow from traditional lenders.

"Jensen out of Nvidia basically was the equivalent of the [US Federal Reserve] raising rates by 50 bits," Dan Ives, technology analyst at merchant bank Yorkville Ives, told SBS' On the Money podcast.

"I mean, he was that important. And I think, [in relation to] the circular financing, he's essential. He is the AI bank."

'Good corporate citizen'

Investors are also weighing a barrage of legal challenges facing Huang and Nvidia.

The board that let Huang go and then rehired him is still overseeing an internal investigation into concerns that he may have been the target of a Chinese espionage campaign, even though Trump says he has been cleared.

The US justice department is separately investigating Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company that allegedly bought Nvidia processors and routed them to Chinese customers in violation of US export restrictions. One of the women Huang had an affair with, Alice Huang (no relation), was an executive at Megaspeed, but stepped down from the role in 2025.

The Securities and Exchange Commission has also reportedly opened an inquiry into Nvidia's accounting practices and potentially misleading communication to shareholders.

"Nvidia is a good corporate citizen. That shouldn't be groundbreaking," US attorney-general Todd Blanche told reporters at an unrelated press conference.

"If Nvidia was the target or was subject to some criminal investigation, or they were obstructing or thwarting our investigation, then that wouldn't be the message that the president is saying to the American people," he added.

Jensen Huang will nevertheless face lawmakers at a closed-door hearing before three House committees on 1 December and a livestreamed Senate committee hearing on 3 December.

"There's gonna be more scrutiny about China and the loophole revenue, but let's just be clear. Jensen is like the pilot on the aeroplane. You don't want the pilot on an aeroplane taking a parachute out mid-flight when you're going into a thunderstorm," Ives said.

Politicians from both parties have expressed anger over the circumstances of Huang's return, and the scrutiny is likely to intensify in January, when Democrats take control of both chambers of Congress.

title: US officials defend plan to destroy unstable explosives in Iowa after Trump pause
text:
In brief Residents near a small Iowa town have been urged to evacuate before the planned destruction of unstable explosives.

The operation has raised concerns about potential lead contamination and public safety.

The United States Army has urged residents of a small Iowa town and nearby areas to evacuate ahead of the planned detonation of some 4,500kg of unstable and degraded explosive material.

The plan — which has sparked fears of lead contamination — is to destroy the country's entire stockpile of lead azide, a material previously used to trigger other explosives in munitions but which officials say is now at risk of spontaneous detonation. The detonation is set for Thursday.

The US Federal Emergency Management Agency is "supporting the recommended relocation for all residents of Middletown, Iowa, and immediate surrounding impacted areas" out of "an abundance of caution", the army said in a public safety advisory. Middletown has a population of around 360.

The destruction of the lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant had been scheduled for 20 November.

But it was postponed by three days, after which US President Donald Trump ordered a pause in the detonation, which is now scheduled to proceed.

On Tuesday, Trump ordered a pause on the planned detonation, saying it would proceed only if an appeals court signed off and if Iowa's incoming governor, Democrat Rob Sand, agreed to let it go ahead.

The court cleared the way for the destruction of the explosives in a ruling on Tuesday, while Sand said the "administration should make this decision based on the information they have from the people they brought in to do the job months ago".

title: The money changes you can make, as Australians told to expect financial pain
text:
in brief Jim Chalmers has warned Australians to brace for stubborn inflation and sustained economic pain in 2027.

Financial experts say auditing recurring household bills and building emergency buffers are among the steps people can take.

With Australians being warned that more economic pain is on the horizon, financial experts are urging households to future-proof their finances before the end of the year.

On Monday, Treasurer Jim Chalmers warned in a rare parliamentary statement that the Australian economy is at a "serious" moment and that serious decisions must be made in response.

"Global and domestic factors, including the ongoing effect of higher interest rates, mean our economy and our people will be under more pressure for longer than we would like," Chalmers told parliament.

"We say with humility and with honesty that things might get a bit harder before they get easier."

The ongoing wars in Iran and Ukraine, rising fuel costs, and debt from the COVID-19 pandemic are all contributing factors to a looming 2027 which the treasurer said will see unemployment and inflation remain high while growth slows.
