As Sam Konstas fell for 11 in another blow to his hopes of a return to the Australian Test side, Queensland batsman Jack Clayton did his best to convince national selectors he’s ready for a call-up. With Marnus Labuschagne already told that he’s not in the selectors’ plans to take on the Black Caps next month, teammate Clayton hit an unbeaten 83 at the Sydney Cricket Ground on Wednesday. It was Clayton’s fifth time past 50 in this year’s Sheffield Shield competition, lifting his season tally to 449 runs at 74.83. Jack Clayton raises his bat after registering a half-century against NSW. Getty Images Fellow Queenslander Mitch Swepson also snared four second-innings scalps, including Konstas with his first ball, to see the Test leg-spinner finish with his third career 10-wicket haul. The 33-year-old’s eye-catching performance came as questions continue to hang over the future of veteran off-spinner Nathan Lyon, who took three wickets for the match but rarely troubled the Bulls’ batsmen on a pitch that Swepson declared was a throwback to the good old days on Tuesday.

Advertisement

“It’s nice to see some footmarks, a bit of bareness in the wicket, some cracking,” said Swepson, who played the last of his four Tests against Sri Lanka in 2022. “My last few games I’ve experienced here, it’s been pretty green, pretty seam friendly, so it’s nice to see some old school characteristics coming back here, particularly at the SCG.” Mitchell Swepson took 10 wickets for the match against NSW at the Sydney Cricket Ground. Getty Images After starting the season with a century, Clayton’s latest half-century could not have come at a better time for the 27-year-old as Australia’s selection panel prepares to meet later this week to pick the squad to take on New Zealand in Perth on December 9. Whether he rockets into calculations could come down to whether selectors persist with Travis Head at the top of the order.

Advertisement

Despite hitting match-winning centuries at the top of the order during last year’s Ashes, as well as a second-inning century against the Proteas in the second Test last month, there have been strong calls for the Test vice-captain to return to the middle order. The dashing left-hander’s three single-digit scores in the recent ODI series against England have only seen those calls sound louder. If he was moved down the order, it would likely be a two-horse race to replace him with Konstas and Jake Weatherald in the mix to return. Sam Konstas looks dejected after being dismissed for 11 against Queensland on day four of the Sheffield Shield. Getty Images While Konstas has the most runs in this year’s Shield season (479 runs at 68.42), the 21-year-old’s bid to return took a slight hit on Wednesday when he belted Swepson to Labuschagne at cover. It continued a miserable outing for the talented youngster, who battled illness throughout the game and was forced to sit away from his teammates. Weatherald, who was dropped following scores of 23 and 0 in the embarrassing loss to Bangladesh in August but still holds a Cricket Australia contract, has moved to fourth on the most runs in this year’s Shield season (386 runs at 48.25) after hitting back-to-back centuries.

But if Head was to remain at the top of the order, selectors could look to bring in a fresh face to bat in the top four, even if Steve Smith, who was bowled by a beauty from Jack Sinfield for 13 on Wednesday, moves up to first-drop and Clayton – a classic left-hander, who is a throwback to an era before T20 – is timing his run to perfection. Clayton, who was a part of the Brisbane Lions’ academy but missed out on the AFL draft, said recently that former Queensland and Australian coach Darren Lehmann had played a pivotal role in his career. “Darren Lehmann was excellent for me in terms of freeing me up and encouraging me to play positive cricket,” Clayton said.

Promises of local jobs at a Queensland government project in Mackay did not eventuate, with CFMEU-backed contractors from Brisbane brought in instead to upgrade the city’s hospital. Vassallo Constructions director Brendan Vassallo told the Commission of Inquiry into the CFMEU and Misconduct in the Construction Industry on Wednesday the company had sought work at the $250 million Mackay Base Hospital upgrade, which has still not been completed. BESIX Watpac had been awarded the contract to deliver the project, and Vassallo met with project director Michael Brady to discuss opportunities. Local contractors say they were locked out of the Mackay Base Hospital upgrade. Given its scale, the former Labor government’s Best Practice Industry Conditions policy applied to the project.

Advertisement

“We worked through what we would need to do,” Vassallo said. “We were told that an EBA of some form would need to be in place, which our company didn’t have at the time. Vassallo Constructions director Brendan Vassallo gave evidence via video link. Commission of Inquiry “Through email discussion and correspondence, we were told that a CFMEU EBA, similar to the EBA in place with Watpac, would be required for us to work on the project.” Vassallo said the company was “a bit taken aback” by the demand, which would have applied to all of the company’s projects, and ultimately decided against it.

Advertisement

The job instead went to a Brisbane-based company, which Vassallo said would have come at a significantly higher cost for Queensland taxpayers. Related Article Graphic content

CFMEU Secret witness tells inquiry about drug-fuelled sex party on Gold Coast “If the contractor needed to bring employees, labour and management from Brisbane and accommodate and pay living-away-from-home allowances and the like, they would have been less commercially competitive than we would have been as a local contractor,” he said. Commissioner Stuart Wood referred to a 2023 media release from then-health minister Shannon Fentiman announcing BESIX Watpac’s contract. “One of the things Ms Fentiman says in her media release is 610 construction jobs, together with 128 extra beds, is a win-win for the region. What do you think about that?” Wood asked, incorrectly attributing the quote to Fentiman rather than then-local MP Julieanne Gilbert.

Advertisement

“For these early works, I can’t say how much was delivered with local contractors and how much was brought in from out of town,” Vassallo said. “But, certainly, if we were given the opportunity to work on the project, it would have been 100 per cent local employees on the project.” Wood said the commission had previously heard that one of BPIC’s objectives was to try to encourage local work. “What do you say about that, if anything?” Wood asked. Vassallo replied: “If it’s the way that it’s played out in our experience, that hasn’t been the case for us.”

Advertisement

Later, former McConnell Dowell human resources manager Michael Kulk gave evidence about his time on the Gold Coast light rail project between 2011 and 2014 as part of the GoldlinQ consortium. Related Article Brisbane 2032 Olympics Olympic venues hit with new construction code as stadium dig hits 100th day Kulk said, during the design and construction phase, the Australian Workers’ Union accounted for about 70 per cent of the project, and negotiations with the AWU had been “fairly amicable”. Dealing with the CFMEU was another matter, Kulk said, particularly when dealing with then-state secretary Michael Ravbar. “[Ravbar’s] belief was that they covered all of the works on the actual worksite,” Kulk said.

Advertisement

“He said he was very disappointed that we had talked to the AWU, and we first should have gone to the CFMEU at that time to form an agreement. “He used words to the effect that we’re pissing in their pocket and the relationship with the CFMEU was obviously on a back foot, in his opinion, to coming to the table to negotiate with them, considering our actions were that we reached an agreement with the AWU before the CFMEU at that time.” Kulk said the CFMEU effectively sought to vet the list of contractors being used on the light rail project, preferring businesses with employees signed up to their union. Fast forward to 2023 and Kulk once again found himself working on the Gold Coast light rail project, this time for Allroads, which also had a $50 million contract with the Queensland Train Manufacturing Program. Allroads did not have an EBA with the CFMEU, Kulk said, and was pressured to apply BPIC standards to all its projects.

In the end, Kulk said, Allroads was unable to enter an agreement with the CFMEU. “Given that it was about $50 million worth of work in hand at that period of time, it would have had a significant contribution to its financial stability in moving forward, and potentially what the banks could have loaned with having those works in hand,” he said. The Albany brothers, 65, from Western Australia's Great Southern, shared a $1m Millionaire Medley prize within two years of winning Set For Life.

The first win helped them buy their sister's home, now they can pay off the property and hit the road.
